title: The Hindenburg Disaster
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart intro voice) cover the 1937 Hindenburg disaster at Lakehurst, New Jersey. They begin with a promo for the Stuff at Sea Virgin Voyages cruise, then explain dirigible types (non-rigid, semi-rigid, rigid), the Hindenburg's construction and hydrogen lift, and the history of airships from Giffard and Zeppelin through LZ 7 and the transatlantic push. They discuss luxury cabins, the bar and the Pauline Charteris drink story, the Nazi-era propaganda flights, and the final flight on May 6, 1937, including the landing, the fire, and Herb Morrison's radio call. The episode closes with sabotage theories (Joseph Spiel/Ben Doova, insurance fraud, incendiary paint, Giappus's capacitor theory), the lasting effect on hydrogen airships, and a listener mail segment.

segments.title: Opening and Stuff at Sea promo
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, promote the Stuff at Sea Virgin Voyages cruise in October, and introduce the Hindenburg topic.

segments.title: Hindenburg overview and what a dirigible is
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the 1937 Lakehurst crash and note the Hindenburg had already flown many flights. They define a dirigible as powered and steerable and note its lift from lighter-than-air gas.

segments.title: Types of airships and Hindenburg construction
segments.summary: They describe non-rigid, semi-rigid, and rigid airships. The Hindenburg's rigid frame used Duralumin, with rings and gas cells covered by cotton fabric coated for UV protection.

segments.title: Passenger gondola and Hindenburg size
segments.summary: The hosts discuss passengers being inside the envelope, and the ship's enormous size compared with a Boeing 747 and its hydrogen capacity.

segments.title: Early airship history: Giffard, Zeppelin, and LZ 7
segments.summary: The hosts trace airship history from Giffard's 1852 airship and the French Army's later dirigible through Zeppelin's first rigid airship in 1900 and the LZ 7 crash in 1910.

segments.title: Transatlantic ambitions and the LZ 127 crossing
segments.summary: They describe Zeppelin's growth and the goal of competing with ocean liners, including the first transatlantic flight in 1928 from Germany to Lakehurst.

segments.title: Luxury transatlantic fleet and fares
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the planned fleet of luxury transatlantic zeppelins, the Hindenburg's wealthy clientele, and fares compared with ocean liners.

segments.title: Hydrogen versus helium decision
segments.summary: The R101 crash in 1930 pushed designers toward helium, but a US helium embargo forced a return to hydrogen, which required more cabins for weight.

segments.title: Hindenburg specs and speed
segments.summary: The hosts list cruising speed, crew and passenger numbers, the 1936 season, and typical cruising altitude.

segments.title: Interior, smoking room, bar, and Pauline Charteris drink
segments.summary: They describe the Art Deco interior, aluminum piano, dining room, smoking room with a single lighter, the bartender, and the story of a cherry-based martini made by Pauline Charteris.

segments.title: Nazi propaganda flights and 1936 season
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Nazi swastikas on the tail, the 1936 publicity tour and maiden voyage, the Olympic propaganda flight, and passengers like Eddie Rickenbacher.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the 1937 flights are described.

segments.title: Final flight and landing at Lakehurst
segments.summary: The hosts recount the May 3 1937 departure from Frankfurt, delays from storms, the evening landing at Lakehurst, and the mooring ropes dropped before the fire.

segments.title: The fire and casualties
segments.summary: The hosts describe the fire starting at the tail, the roughly 34 seconds of destruction, the ground crew death, and that about two thirds of the 97 people aboard survived.

segments.title: Herb Morrison radio broadcast
segments.summary: Chuck reads from Herb Morrison's famous Chicago radio call, and the hosts discuss the origin of the phrase Oh the humanity.

segments.title: Immediate response and early theories
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Navy rescue response and early sabotage theories tied to Nazis, communists, and anarchists.

segments.title: Joseph Spiel suspect and 1975 film
segments.summary: They discuss suspect Joseph Spiel (Ben Doova), the steward's suspicion, the insurance fraud theory, and the 1975 film The Hindenburg.

segments.title: Incendiary paint theory and Addison Bain
segments.summary: Addison Bain's incendiary paint theory is described, along with his television demonstration that was later debunked.

segments.title: Giappus capacitor theory
segments.summary: The hosts describe Caltech professor Constantinos Giappus's theory that electrostatic charge built up between the skin and frame, and its NOVA test.

segments.title: Legacy: end of hydrogen airships and modern airships
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the disaster ended transatlantic airships and hydrogen fuel interest, modern helium airships such as the Pathfinder backed by Sergey Brin, and a debunked survivor myth.

segments.title: Museum artifacts
segments.summary: Chuck mentions Hindenburg artifacts at the Smithsonian and the National Air and Space Museum.

segments.title: Listener mail from Michael in Columbus
segments.summary: A listener from Columbus, Ohio, praises the show and says he started listening at age ten.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and the iHeartRadio production note.
